observations: body L1-L16: Schiaparelli's addition begun on p. 241 goes on here; a heavy bracket closes it in L16, after a dash of 9.7 pt.
body L4, L8, L18, L20, L30, L34: «al-Battānī» in L4 has a hyphen (3.5 pt) and is not letter-spaced; the dashes of «al–Battānī» in the other lines are long dashes (5.2 to 5.3 pt).

body L13-L14: Ptolemy puts the apogee of Venus at Taurus 25° (Almagest X, 1) and that of the Sun, fixed, at Gemini 5° 30′ (III, 4): in his own time they are 10° 30′ apart. About 20° (19° 20′) is their distance at the epoch of Nabonassar, where the apogee of Venus is 46° 10′ (p. 241, L3).

body L14, L16-L18, L31: the dashes after «(1).», before «Schiaparelli», after «III.» and «maiores.» and after «312.» measure 9.7 to 10.2 pt; those of «12–15» and «879–880» 5.4 and 4.2 pt, transcribed as long dashes.

body L19-L22: the motions of al-Battānī are 37 times those of 20 Julian years in his table (Part II, p. 103: Venus 183° 43′ 2″, Mercury 14° 27′ 43″ 20‴). Ptolemy's daily motions in anomaly (Almagest IX, 3: 0;36,59,25,53,11,28 and 3;6,24,6,59,35,50) give in the 270285 days of 740 Julian years 313° 3′ 47″ 17‴ 39⁗ for Venus and 174° 9′ 3″ 0‴ 35⁗ for Mercury. The printed «16‴» of Venus is 1‴ 39⁗ short, and the difference of Venus would be 4° 28′ 26″ 42‴; the printed «44‴» is right for 16‴. The figures for Mercury and their difference are right. The rules under Ptolemy's numbers print broken.
body L25-L26: Ptolemy's daily motion gives in 365 days 225° 1′ 32″ 28‴ 34⁗ 45⁵, as printed to the fourths; the IV of the fourths is printed in small capitals.
body L27-L28: the head of chapter 32 is set in the larger type of the heads.
body L28-L29: in the head the dash after «a)» measures 9.8 pt, that of «16–22» 6.5 pt; the dash of «’l–qarnayn» is a long dash (5.3 pt).
body L29, L34: the names of the eras, «Aera Alexandri Dhū ’l–qarnayn» and «Aera Alexandri Macedonis», are set in letter-spaced italics.
body L30-L31: 1 October 312 B.C. (Julian calendar) was a Monday and 1 September 312 B.C. a Saturday.
body L33: the sign of equality before «Septembri» is 9.4 pt long.
body L35: the second letter of «κκνόνες» is printed as a kappa where κανόνες has an alpha; kept as printed.
body L6-L7, L22: specks under the S of «Solem» (L6), above the space between «tunc» and «deferentem» (L7) and before the «0°» of the differences (L22) are not transcribed.

notes_left L2: the c of «adn. c» is bold italic; the hyphen of «216-18» measures 2.6 pt; the closing parenthesis after «18» prints broken, like a semicolon, and the hyphen of «apo-» prints as a raised dot.
notes_left L4: note 2 goes on in the right column. «XVIII, 82» is Flügel's numbering of the verse (83 in the Cairo numbering).

notes_left L4: the addenda (Part I, p. LXXIV) on note 2: Nallino had explained the name after several scholars, above all because Clement of Alexandria complains that Alexander had himself portrayed in the image of a god, with horns. Its true origin is shown by Fr. Kampers, Alexander der Grosse und die Idee des Weltimperiums in Prophetie und Sage, Freiburg i. Br. 1901, p. 71–85 (Studien und Darstellungen aus dem Gebiete der Geschichte, ed. H. Grauert, fasc. II–III). In the legends of Alexander current in the East, especially among the Syrians, in the first centuries of the Christian era, Alexander appears as the restorer of a new age and saviour of the world, like the Messiah of the Hebrews; he is therefore given the two horns that Jewish writings call the sign of the Messiah. All this comes from very ancient Babylonian beliefs, set out briefly in E. Schrader, Die Keilinschriften und das Alte Testament, 3rd ed. by H. Zimmern and H. Winckler, Berlin 1902, p. 380–82; for the same reason Naram-Sin, king of Babylonia, was represented with two horns 25 centuries before Alexander.
